content:
Apple's lawsuit against OpenAI deliberately distances former design chief Jony Ive from the case—but that may not stop him from being dragged in. Here's why.

OpenAI has a chance to put Apple in a very awkward position.

In its complaint accusing OpenAI of trade secret theft, Apple conspicuously avoids naming Ive. His company, io Products, is at the center of the hardware collaboration with OpenAI that Apple is now suing over.

At one point, the complaint accuses "OpenAI and its co-conspirators of institutional wrongdoing," naming io among them but describing it only as "a company co-founded by Mr. Tang and other former Apple executives." Beyond that, the filing doesn't mention Ive, Evans Hankey, or any other former Apple executives by name—except Tang Tan and Chang Liu, who are directly accused of wrongdoing.

It's too early to say whether Ive will be called to testify, but it's a real possibility—especially if OpenAI puts him on the stand to embarrass or corner Apple.

That would put Apple in a uniquely delicate position. Since leaving in 2019, Ive has publicly maintained a posture of respect toward his former employer, carefully managing his public appearances and visits.

That includes events alongside Laurene Powell Jobs and his ongoing involvement with the Steve Jobs Archive. Earlier this year, Ive hand-wrote a letter for the archive's "Letters to a Young Creator" series, reflecting on his years working with Steve Jobs.

Apple, for its part, has appeared to reciprocate that respect—delicately walking back a number of controversial decisions from Ive's final years, including the MacBook's butterfly keyboard. Its apparent effort to keep him at arm's length from this lawsuit fits squarely with that approach.

But once the case enters discovery, Apple won't have full control over who gets pulled in. Given Ive's role in founding io Products and overseeing the hardware project at the heart of the dispute, OpenAI could argue he has relevant knowledge about how the product was developed, what information the team relied on, and whether Apple's trade secrets were involved.

That could set up an uncomfortable moment for Apple: questioning Ive on the stand, challenging his account, or trying to undermine the credibility of the executive who shaped some of Apple's most iconic products.

It wouldn't be Ive's first time testifying in litigation involving Apple. Back in 2012, he was deposed in Apple's patent suit against Samsung, answering questions about Apple's design process and early iPhone and iPad prototypes.

But testifying on the opposing side this time could strain the relationship he's carefully preserved with Apple—and potentially sour things with OpenAI, too, if Ive feels the company roped him into a fight with his former employer unnecessarily.

Do you think Jony Ive will get pulled into this lawsuit? Let us know in the comments.
